newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rain hits wheat yields, quality in eastern France.
newsitem.headline: Rain hits wheat yields, quality in eastern France.

text.p: The soft wheat harvest is now 75-80 percent complete in the Bourgogne Franche-Comte region in eastern France and initial cuts suggest June rain and sporadic showers this month hit crop yields and quality, local crop analysts said on Thursday.
More showers forecast for the coming days are also expected to slow down farmers' progress, possibly worsening the crop condition, they said.
"The wheat harvest may very well drag into early August," an official from the local ONIC grain office in Dijon said.
But the winter barley crop fared better because it had already reached maturity when the rain hit the region. The harvest is now 98 percent complete.
This led local crop officials to revise downwards their pre-harvest forecasts for soft wheat yields and to adjust upwards estimates for winter barley yields.

The latest assumptions are now for a soft wheat yield in line or slightly lower than the 6.2 tonnes per hectare reached last year. This compares with a previous estimate of 6.3 tonnes for 1997 soft wheat yields.
Winter barley yields may be revised upwards to 5.8 tonnes from a pre-harvest estimate of 5.7 tonnes and 5.7 tonnes reached last year.
But the region will produce more soft wheat and barley than last year because sowings are on the rise, crop officials said.
"The crops largely recovered from a spring drought but the rain since June has been the main problem," one official said.

High moisture levels led to unwanted wheat germination in an estimated two percent of the fields. The rain also pushed down specific weight and sparked the outbreak of diseases, mostly fungi that attack the leaves and threaten yields.
Fears that the spring drought might push up protein content and disqualify a large part of the barley crop for malting have now eased.
"Protein content ranges from 9.5 to 13 percent but we estimate that some 70 percent of the barley crop will be fit for malting," the analyst said.
